To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) networks often exhibit hierarchical structure, in which vertices are grouped into clusters, which are further grouped into clusters of clusters, and so forth, over many scales, (ii) the existence of hierarchical structure in a network is sufficient to quantitatively explain many commonly observed network topological properties such as right skewed distributions of vertex degrees, high clustering coefficients, short path lengths, and (iii) the existence of hierarchy in a network can be used to accurately predict missing links in the network, and

(1) hierarchical structure is a common feature of networks, (2) hierarchical structure can be inferred from network data, (3) hierarchical structure can explain many commonly observed properties of networks, (4) hierarchical structure can improve the prediction of missing connections in networks, (5) hierarchical structure is more generally useful than competing techniques for the prediction of missing edges in networks, (6) hierarchical structure can predict missing connections in networks that do not have the same degree distributions as the networks on which hierarchical structure

hierarchical structure is a general organizing principle of complex systems and that the presence of hierarchy is capable of explaining and quantitatively reproducing many of the most common topological properties of complex networks.
